name: Adult-onset Still disease
aliases: systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis adult equivalent
systemic-onset juvenile idiopathic arthritis in adults

clinicalPearls: Classic triad is quotidian (once- or twice-daily) high spiking fever, evanescent salmon-pink rash that appears with fever spikes, and arthritis/arthralgia
Rash is typically truncal and on proximal limbs, non-pruritic, and often elicited or worsened by scratching (Koebner-like phenomenon)
Sore throat and cervical lymphadenopathy are common early features and can mimic infection
Markedly elevated ferritin, often more than five times normal, is a strong clue but not specific
Rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibody are typically negative, helping distinguish AOSD from other connective tissue diseases
Neutrophilic leukocytosis with left shift and elevated inflammatory markers accompany the fever spikes
Diagnosis is one of exclusion after infections, malignancy, and other rheumatologic diseases are ruled out
Watch for macrophage activation syndrome, a life-threatening complication marked by falling counts and rapidly rising ferritin
harrison.pathophysiology: AOSD is an autoinflammatory disorder driven by innate immune activation rather than autoantibody-mediated disease, with overproduction of proinflammatory cytokines including interleukin-1, interleukin-6, interleukin-18, and tumor necrosis factor. This cytokine storm produces the systemic febrile illness, marked acute-phase response, and hyperferritinemia seen clinically. The absence of a clear autoantibody or defined trigger, along with strong similarity to systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, supports its classification as an autoinflammatory rather than autoimmune condition.
additionalDifferentials: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms
nonInfectiousMimics: Familial Mediterranean fever and other periodic fever syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Serum ferritin and glycosylated ferritin fraction — marked elevation with low glycosylated fraction supports diagnosis
Complete blood count with differential — neutrophilic leukocytosis typical; cytopenias raise concern for macrophage activation syndrome
Liver function tests — transaminitis is common
Blood cultures and viral serologies — to exclude infectious mimics before immunosuppression
ANA and rheumatoid factor — expected negative, helps exclude other connective tissue disease
Imaging or lymph node biopsy — to exclude lymphoma when lymphadenopathy is prominent
Joint imaging — assess for erosive arthritis, notably of the wrist, in chronic disease
Triglycerides, fibrinogen, soluble CD25/IL-2 receptor — screen for macrophage activation syndrome if clinical deterioration occurs
redFlags: Cytopenias, coagulopathy, or precipitous rise in ferritin suggesting macrophage activation syndrome
Hepatic failure or disseminated intravascular coagulation
Adult respiratory distress syndrome from pulmonary involvement
Persistent fever despite broad antimicrobial coverage without an identified infectious source
pitfalls: Treating as fever of unknown origin with prolonged empiric antibiotics before considering an autoinflammatory cause
Missing the diagnosis because the evanescent rash is absent at the time of examination
Anchoring on markedly elevated ferritin as diagnostic without excluding lymphoma and macrophage activation syndrome
Delaying immunosuppressive therapy while pursuing an exhaustive infectious workup in a clinically deteriorating patient
harrison.prognosis: Course is variable: some patients have a self-limited monophasic illness, others a chronic intermittent pattern, and a subset develop chronic destructive polyarthritis. Most patients respond well to anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive therapy, though macrophage activation syndrome significantly increases morbidity and mortality.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Chapter on Rheumatoid Arthritis and related autoinflammatory/systemic rheumatic disease section covering Adult-onset Still disease
